units.text: Disparities in Breast Reconstruction After Mastectomy in Southeast Asia: A Systematic Review
| Introduction

Breast cancer poses a significant public health challenge in Southeast Asia, where it is the most commonly diagnosed cancer among women.In this region, breast cancer incidence rates (ASIR) are rising rapidly, with an estimated 25-72 new cases per 100 000 women annually (ASIR: Singapore 72.6, Philippines 60.3, Brunei 50.2, Malaysia 46.1, Indonesia 41.8, Vietnam 38.0, Thailand 37.4, Laos 31.6,Cambodia 25.1, and Myanmar 23.4) [1,2].In total, there were approximately 168 500 new cases of breast cancer in Southeast Asia in 2022 [2].This trend is driven by factors such as aging populations, shifts in reproductive behaviors, and changes in diet and physical activity levels.Unfortunately, breast cancer in lower income countries in Southeast Asia is often diagnosed at later stages, with studies showing that up to 50% of cases are detected at Stage III or IV [1].This late diagnosis contributes to a breast cancer mortality-toincidence ratio, defined as the number of deaths that occurs compared to the number of breast cancers diagnosed each year, that can be as high as 0.52 in many Southeast Asian countries, compared to the 0.28 world average [1].

Breast reconstruction is a critical component of breast cancer treatment, particularly, for the approximate 43%-59% of women in Southeast Asia who undergo mastectomy as part of their cancer management [3,4].Mastectomy can have profound psychological and emotional impacts, with studies indicating that up to 60% of women experience body image dissatisfaction postmastectomy, and many report feelings of diminished femininity and decreased self-esteem [5].Breast reconstruction offers a pathway to restore appearance, with evidence showing that women who undergo reconstruction report significant improvements in their quality of life [6].Reconstruction can reduce the psychological distress associated with breast cancer treatment, help women regain a sense of normalcy, and enhance overall satisfaction with their post-cancer body image [6].

Despite its benefits, access to breast reconstruction in Southeast Asia remains limited.In some countries, less than 20% of eligible women undergo reconstruction, largely due to a combination of cultural, economic, and healthcare-related barriers [7].For instance, in Malaysia, a study found that only 36.8% of women undergoing mastectomy were offered reconstruction, and the uptake was even lower among older and less educated women [8].Economic constraints are also a significant barrier, with advanced reconstruction techniques often being prohibitively expensive and concentrated in urban centers, leaving rural women with fewer options [9].These disparities highlight the need for targeted interventions to ensure that all women in Southeast Asia can access the full spectrum of breast cancer care, including reconstruction, to improve their physical and emotional well-being after treatment.

The motivation for exploring disparities in breast reconstruction within Southeast Asia stems from the region's significant and growing burden of breast cancer, coupled with the uneven access to reconstruction services that can profoundly affect patient outcomes [10].Breast cancer is not only the most prevalent cancer among women in Southeast Asia but also one of the leading causes of cancer-related mortality [10].Despite the advancements in cancer treatment and the known benefits of breast reconstruction in enhancing the quality of life postmastectomy, a substantial number of women in this region do not have access to these services [11].This lack of access is influenced by a complex interplay of cultural, economic, and healthcare system factors that vary widely across different countries and even within regions of the same country.

In many parts of Southeast Asia, cultural beliefs and social stigmas about body image, surgery, and cancer recovery contribute to the low uptake of breast reconstruction [12].Economic barriers, such as the prohibitive cost of advanced reconstruction techniques and the lack of financial support or insurance coverage, further limit access, particularly, for women from low-income backgrounds [13,14].Additionally, disparities in healthcare infrastructure mean that even when reconstruction is available, it is often concentrated in urban centers, leaving rural women underserved [15].These disparities lead to unequal treatment outcomes, with some women missing the benefits of reconstruction that could significantly improve their physical and psychological recovery.

The specific aims of this systematic review are to identify and analyze the trends, disparities, and outcomes associated with breast reconstruction in Southeast Asia.The review seeks to examine how the rates and types of breast reconstruction have evolved over time in different Southeast Asian countries, and how these trends compare with global patterns.We also explore the disparities in access to breast reconstruction based on factors such as ethnicity, age, economic status, geographic location, and cultural beliefs.Finally, we seek to evaluate the outcomes of breast reconstruction, including complication rates, patient satisfaction, esthetic results, and oncological safety, with a focus on how these outcomes vary across different demographic and socioeconomic groups.

By achieving these aims, the review aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the factors influencing breast reconstruction in Southeast Asia and to identify areas where targeted interventions and policy changes could improve access and outcomes for all women in the region.
| Methods
| Study Selection and Inclusion Criteria

To conduct a comprehensive systematic review of disparities in breast reconstruction across Southeast Asia, we performed an extensive literature search using multiple databases, including PubMed, Embase, and Scopus.The search strategy was designed to capture a broad spectrum of studies related to breast reconstruction in the region.We utilized search terms that included combinations of keywords such as "breast reconstruction," "mastectomy," "breast cancer," "Southeast Asia," "Vietnam," "Thailand," "Malaysia," "Singapore," "Brunei," "reconstruction disparities," "cultural factors," "economic factors," "surgical outcomes," and "patient satisfaction."Boolean operators (AND, OR) refined the search, ensuring the results were comprehensive and focused on the region and topics of interest.The PRISMA guidelines were used to create this review (Figure 1).

Studies were included in the review if they met specific inclusion criteria.These criteria were as follows: the study had to be conducted in Southeast Asia, specifically in countries such as Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, and Brunei; the study population needed to include women who underwent or were eligible for breast reconstruction following mastectomy for breast cancer; and the study design could be either quantitative (e.g., cohort studies, cross-sectional studies, clinical trials) or qualitative (e.g., interviews, focus groups) to provide a comprehensive understanding of the topic.Additionally, the studies needed to address disparities in access to breast reconstruction, the types of reconstruction techniques used, complication rates, patient satisfaction, or oncological outcomes.We considered studies published between 2000 and 2023 to capture both historical and contemporary practices, and only studies published in English were included due to the language proficiency of the research team.

Studies were excluded if they focused solely on populations outside Southeast Asia, did not address breast reconstruction following mastectomy, or were case reports, reviews, or editorials without original data.After running the search and removing duplicates, the remaining articles were screened based on their titles and abstracts.Articles that appeared relevant were then assessed in full text to confirm their eligibility according to the inclusion criteria.Two independent reviewers assessed each article to ensure consistency and objectivity in the selection process.Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer if necessary.Studies that met the inclusion criteria and were deemed relevant and of sufficient quality were included in the final review (Figure 1).
| Data Extraction and Thematic Analysis

Data extraction from the selected studies was conducted using a standardized data extraction form designed to capture key details such as the study's geographic location, population characteristics, study design, types of breast reconstruction techniques employed, reported outcomes (e.g., complication rates, patient satisfaction), and identified disparities (e.g., cultural, economic, geographic).This process was conducted independently by two reviewers to minimize bias and ensure the accuracy of the extracted information.

Following data extraction, thematic analysis was employed to identify and analyze patterns or themes within the data.Thematic analysis was chosen as it allows for a systematic exploration of recurring themes related to disparities in breast reconstruction across the studies [16].The process began with familiarization, where the research team reviewed the extracted data multiple times to identify preliminary themes and patterns.This was followed by coding, where key elements from each study were systematically categorized to highlight significant themes such as cultural influences on reconstruction decisions, economic barriers to accessing reconstruction, and the impact of geographic location on the availability of advanced surgical techniques.Through this approach, we synthesized the data into coherent themes that provide a deeper understanding of the factors influencing breast reconstruction disparities in Southeast Asia.

| Cultural and Ethnic Disparities

Cultural and ethnic factors play a significant role in influencing breast reconstruction rates and preferences in Southeast Asia.These disparities are shaped by deeply rooted cultural beliefs, varying levels of awareness about reconstruction options, and differences in healthcare access and communication.

In Singapore, Sim et al. highlighted stark ethnic disparities in breast reconstruction rates [17].In this study, Chinese women, despite being the majority of the population in Singapore, accounted for less than 50% of breast reconstructions.The study suggested that cultural beliefs, including the perception of body image and the acceptance of surgical interventions, contributed to these differences.Malay women showed a strong preference for autologous tissue reconstruction (92.3%), which may reflect cultural norms valuing natural body restoration.The Chinese population's lower rates of reconstruction may stem from traditional beliefs about body integrity and surgery, leading to a preference for nonsurgical treatments or avoiding reconstruction altogether [18].

Similarly, Shameem, Yip, and Fong explored cultural influences on breast reconstruction in Malaysia and found that fear of additional surgery and potential complications were significant barriers, especially among older and less educated women [8].The study noted that younger and married women were more likely to choose reconstruction, driven by cultural expectations around femininity and the desire to maintain a sense of normalcy in their appearance.However, the overall low rate of reconstruction offered to patients (36.8%) indicated that cultural reluctance toward surgical intervention, combined with a lack of information, played a significant role in shaping these decisions [8].

The impact of cultural and linguistic diversity on reconstruction decisions is further emphasized in the study by Soon et al. [19] conducted in Australia.This qualitative study examined Vietnamese-speaking and English-speaking women's experiences with breast reconstruction postmastectomy.It found that Vietnamese-speaking women were significantly more likely to report a lack of information about reconstruction as a barrier, compared to their English-speaking counterparts [19].This linguistic barrier, coupled with cultural differences in perceiving breast reconstruction, contributed to lower rates of reconstruction among Vietnamese women.The study also revealed that while both groups valued the ability to wear chosen clothing and the influence of their partners in decisionmaking, Vietnamese women placed particular importance on their doctor's recommendation.This underscores the role of healthcare providers in bridging cultural and linguistic gaps to ensure informed decision-making [19].

Overall, these studies demonstrate that cultural and ethnic factors are deeply intertwined with the decision-making process for breast reconstruction in Southeast Asia.Addressing these disparities requires culturally sensitive communication, better education about reconstruction options, and proactive engagement from healthcare providers to ensure that all women, regardless of their cultural background, have access to informed and equitable breast cancer care.
| Economic and Geographic Disparities

Economic and geographic factors significantly influence access to breast reconstruction across Southeast Asia, often determining whether patients can afford or even consider reconstructive surgery after mastectomy.These disparities manifest in several ways, including the availability of resources, the cost of procedures, and the frequency of surgeon referrals, all of which contribute to uneven access to care.

In Malaysia, Ishak, Yahya, and Halim conducted a cross-sectional survey that highlighted the economic and referral barriers affecting breast reconstruction rates [20].The study revealed that only 86.7% of surgeons discussed reconstruction options with their patients, but the actual referral rates for reconstruction were strikingly low, with an average of just four patients referred for reconstruction over 3 years.This low referral rate was partly attributed to the perception that patients could not afford the additional cost of reconstruction or that they were not interested in the procedure.The study also identified a lack of awareness and education about reconstruction options, which, coupled with financial constraints, limited patients' ability to pursue reconstructive surgery [20].

Similarly, in Singapore, Lim, Low, and Hoe found that economic factors played a critical role in shaping surgeons' decisions to refer patients for breast reconstruction [7].The postal survey of general surgeons revealed that many surgeons were hesitant to recommend reconstruction due to concerns about the cost and the potential burden on patients.Additionally, the study noted that many surgeons were unsure whether reconstruction might mask cancer recurrence, further reducing the likelihood of referrals.This uncertainty, combined with financial considerations, contributed to lower rates of breast reconstruction in Singapore compared to Western countries, where reconstruction is more commonly offered as part of standard breast cancer care [7].

In Vietnam, Dinh Nguyen explored the impact of economic and geographic barriers on breast reconstruction, particularly, in a setting where late-stage breast cancer is prevalent.The retrospective study found that breast reconstruction was primarily performed for early-stage cancer cases, with limited access to reconstruction for those diagnosed at later stages [21].The excessive cost of reconstruction and the uneven distribution of surgical expertise across the country were significant barriers.Many patients, particularly, those in rural areas, lacked access to specialized care and were unable to afford the procedures, leading to a lower overall rate of reconstruction [21].

Nor et al. These studies collectively highlight the pervasive impact of economic and geographic disparities on breast reconstruction access in Southeast Asia.Financial barriers, coupled with the uneven availability of specialized care, particularly, in rural areas, significantly limit patients' options for reconstruction.To address these disparities, there is a need for policies that increase funding for breast cancer care, improve the distribution of medical resources, and enhance education and referral practices among healthcare providers.Ensuring equitable access to reconstruction services is crucial for improving the overall quality of breast cancer care in the region.
| Age and Stage of Disease

Age and the stage of breast cancer at diagnosis are critical factors influencing the likelihood of undergoing breast reconstruction in Southeast Asia.These factors not only affect the decision-making process for both patients and surgeons but also have significant implications for the outcomes of reconstructive surgery.

In Singapore, Ng et al. [23] conducted a comprehensive retrospective review of postmastectomy breast reconstruction trends over a 12-year period.The study found that younger patients, particularly, those under 50 years old, were significantly more likely to undergo breast reconstruction compared to older patients [23].This trend reflects a broader concern among younger women about body image and the psychosocial impacts of mastectomy.

The study also highlighted that patients with early-stage breast cancer were more likely to choose immediate reconstruction, likely due to their generally better prognosis and the desire to minimize the visible impact of cancer treatment.However, for older patients and those with more advanced cancer stages, the likelihood of opting for reconstruction decreased, possibly due to concerns about the risks of additional surgery, longer recovery times, and the potential delay of adjuvant therapies [23].

Yap et al. [24] also examined the influence of age on breast reconstruction outcomes in a prospective study focusing on the DIEP flap procedure in Singapore.Older patients and those with higher BMIs faced increased risks of complications, such as fat necrosis and partial flap loss, which led to disparities in access to DIEP flap reconstruction due to surgeon hesitancy in offering this technique to higher-risk patients [24].The study noted that these risks were more pronounced in older patients, leading to a more cautious approach to offering reconstruction to this demographic.The findings underscore the need for personalized treatment plans that consider the patient's age and overall health status, balancing the benefits of reconstruction with the potential for increased surgical risks [24].

In Thailand, Sattaratnamai, Samankatiwat, and Lohsiriwat explored the impact of both age and cancer stage on surgical choices, including breast reconstruction.Their retrospective cohort study revealed that younger patients and those with early-stage disease were more likely to undergo breastconserving surgery (BCS) or immediate breast reconstruction (MTIBR) [25].In contrast, older patients and those diagnosed with advanced-stage cancer were more likely to undergo mastectomy without reconstruction.The study attributed this trend to several factors, including the more aggressive treatment required for advanced cancer and the higher perceived risks of complications in older patients.Additionally, the availability of surgical options, influenced by the surgeon's training and experience, played a role in determining whether reconstruction was offered [25].

These studies collectively highlight the strong influence of age and cancer stage on the decision to undergo breast reconstruction in Southeast Asia.Younger patients and those diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer are more likely to pursue reconstruction, often motivated by concerns about body image, quality of life, and the desire to recover their pre-cancer appearance.Conversely, older patients and those with more advanced disease face greater barriers, both in terms of the physical risks associated with surgery and the availability of appropriate surgical options.Addressing these disparities requires a nuanced approach that considers the individual patient's health status, preferences, and the stage of their disease, ensuring that all patients have access to informed and appropriate reconstructive options.
| Trends in Surgical Techniques and Patient Outcomes

The deep inferior epigastric perforator (DIEP) and (Transverse Rectus Abdominis Myocutaneous [TRAM]) flaps are widely used in Southeast Asia for breast reconstruction due to their ability to create a natural-looking breast mound using the patient's own tissue [26,27].These techniques have been studied extensively in different contexts within the region.

In Vietnam, Nguyen et al. conducted a prospective study evaluating the outcomes of DIEP flap reconstructions.The study found that the overall flap success rate was 90%, with 40% of patients experiencing complications, including venous congestion and fat necrosis [28].Patient satisfaction was high, with 88.9% of patients expressing satisfaction with their breasts 1 month postoperation.This study underscores the DIEP flap's effectiveness in creating esthetically pleasing outcomes while also highlighting the technical nuances that can impact complication rates.However, access to DIEP flap reconstruction was largely limited to patients with early-stage cancer, with rural and lower-income patients less likely to undergo this advanced technique due to limited availability and high costs [28].

In Singapore, Tan et al. [29] compared the DIEP flap with the pedicled TRAM flap, focusing on cost-effectiveness and complication rates.The high cost of the DIEP flap limited its accessibility, particularly, for lower-income patients, who were more likely to receive the older, more cost-effective TRAM flap despite its higher complication rates [29].The total hospitalization cost for the DIEP flap was significantly higher than for the TRAM flap (SGD 11 009.38 vs. SGD 8300.51,p < 0.001).However, both techniques showed comparable outcomes in terms of patient satisfaction and esthetic results.The study's findings suggest that while the DIEP flap offers some advantages in reducing complications, the TRAM flap's costeffectiveness makes it a viable option, particularly, in settings where resources are limited [29].This cost comparison is further illustrated in Figure 2.

Patient satisfaction with the esthetic outcomes of breast reconstruction is intricately linked to the type of reconstruction performed and the occurrence of complications.In Brunei, Nor et al. [22] conducted a multi-method study to assess patient satisfaction following breast reconstruction.The study found that overall satisfaction was high, with a median score of 80.5 [22].

Patients expressed the highest satisfaction with surgical care and the doctor-patient relationship, indicating that the quality of care and communication played a significant role in their perception of the outcomes.However, satisfaction with specific aspects of the reconstruction, such as nipple reconstruction, was lower, with a mean score of 32.7.This suggests that while the general esthetic outcome was positively received, specific areas of the reconstruction process, particularly, those involving intricate details like nipple reconstruction, may require further refinement to enhance patient satisfaction [22].

In Malaysia, Shameem, Yip, and Fong examined the reasons behind women's decisions to undergo or decline breast reconstruction, as well as their satisfaction with the esthetic outcomes.The study found that women who chose to undergo reconstruction were generally motivated by the desire to "feel whole again" and regain their femininity [8].Among those who opted for reconstruction, the esthetic outcomes were largely satisfactory, contributing to a sense of restored self-image and confidence.However, the study also highlighted that fear of complications, such as infections and poor esthetic results, was a significant barrier for those who declined the procedure.This fear was, particularly, pronounced among older women, who were less likely to pursue reconstruction due to concerns about their ability to recover from potential complications [8].

These studies collectively illustrate the complex relationship between complication rates and esthetic outcomes in breast reconstruction across Southeast Asia.While advancements in surgical techniques have improved the ability to achieve natural-looking results, the risk of complications like necrosis and infection remains a significant challenge.Patient satisfaction is highly dependent on both the immediate esthetic outcome and the longer-term durability of the reconstruction.As such, it is essential for surgeons to carefully weigh the risks and benefits of each reconstruction technique, provide clear communication about potential complications, and offer ongoing support to patients as they navigate their postsurgical recovery and esthetic expectations.
| Oncological Safety and Long-Term Outcomes

The oncological safety of breast reconstruction is a paramount concern, particularly, in regions like Southeast Asia, where access to specialized cancer care can vary widely [30].Studies from Vietnam and Thailand have provided valuable insights into how different reconstruction methods influence survival rates and recurrence, shedding light on the long-term safety and efficacy of these procedures (Tables 2-4).

In      findings were encouraging: the 5-year overall survival rate was reported at 95%, with a 5-year disease-free survival rate of 80.7%.Importantly, the study found that early diagnosis and treatment were crucial in achieving these high survival rates.The low recurrence rates observed in this cohort suggest that when performed on carefully selected patients, both the LD and TRAM flap reconstructions can be safely integrated into comprehensive breast cancer treatment plans without compromising oncological outcomes [21].

Sriussadaporn and Angspatt provided a detailed analysis of the long-term outcomes associated with skin-sparing mastectomy (SSM) followed by immediate reconstruction in early breast cancer patients in Thailand [31].The study included 14 patients who underwent this combined procedure, with a follow-up period ranging from 6 to 50 months (mean 26.5 months).While the procedure was successful in early-stage breast cancer patients, access to immediate reconstruction remained limited, particularly, for patients diagnosed at later stages, exacerbating disparities in long-term outcomes.Additionally, there were no cases of skin flap necrosis, hematoma, or major complications that could compromise the oncological or esthetic outcomes.These findings underscore the potential of SSM with immediate reconstruction to provide both oncological safety and satisfactory esthetic results, making it a viable option for women with early breast cancer who are candidates for this approach [31].
| Discussion
| Synthesis of Key Findings

The systematic review of breast reconstruction in Southeast Asia reveals a complex interplay between disparities in access, the choice of surgical techniques, and patient outcomes.These disparities are deeply influenced by cultural, economic, and medical factors, which together shape the landscape of breast reconstruction in the region.Understanding these interconnections is essential for improving breast cancer care and ensuring that reconstruction is accessible and effective for all patients, regardless of their background or circumstances.Figure 2 highlights the key barriers to breast reconstruction in Southeast Asia, ranked by prominence based on a systematic review of the literature.Each barrier was rated on a scale from 1 (low) to 5 (very high), reflecting its impact on access to care.Economic barriers were the most prominent, with high costs (ranked 5) and lack of insurance or financial support (ranked 4) posing significant challenges.Additionally, the urban concentration of services (ranked 4) exacerbates disparities, as rural women face greater financial and logistical hurdles.Cultural barriers, such as the stigma around surgery (ranked 5) and fear of complications (ranked 4), deter women from seeking reconstruction, particularly, in older and less educated populations.Cultural beliefs around body image and surgery play a significant role in decision-making.The lack of information, including awareness gaps (ranked 4) and language barriers (ranked 3), further restricts access, especially in rural or underserved areas where women are less informed about reconstruction options.Finally, healthcare infrastructure limitations, such as geographic disparities (ranked 4) and the shortage of trained surgeons (ranked 5), contribute to unequal  2, Table 5).
| Disparities in Access and Surgical Techniques

One of the most significant findings from the reviewed studies is the pronounced disparity in access to breast reconstruction, driven largely by cultural and economic factors.Cultural beliefs, as highlighted in studies like Sim et al. and Soon et al., play a crucial role in shaping patient decisions about reconstruction [17,19].In many Southeast Asian cultures, traditional views on body integrity and the stigma associated with surgical alterations contribute to lower rates of reconstruction.For example, in Singapore, cultural preferences among different ethnic groups led to varying rates of reconstruction, with Malay women showing a stronger preference for autologous tissue reconstruction compared to Chinese women, who were more hesitant about surgery due to cultural beliefs about body integrity (Figure 3).[20] Limited awareness and misconceptions Many women did not opt for reconstruction because they were not informed or held incorrect beliefs about the risks and benefits Malaysia Ng et al. (2016) [23] Gender roles and expectations Younger women, especially those concerned about body image and societal expectations, were more likely to undergo reconstruction Singapore Sattaratnamai et al.

(2018) [25] Perceived necessity of maintaining body integrity Older women were more likely to avoid reconstruction, preferring to preserve their natural body Thailand constraints limit access to reconstruction, particularly, in resourcelimited settings like Malaysia and Vietnam [7,20].Excessive costs, coupled with a lack of insurance coverage and financial support, prevent many women from opting for reconstruction.This economic barrier is closely tied to the availability of specialized surgical techniques.In regions where healthcare resources are limited, advanced techniques like the DIEP flap may be less accessible, leading to reliance on older, more cost-effective methods like the TRAM flap.However, as shown in Tan et al., even when newer techniques are available, their higher cost can be a deterrent, further entrenching disparities [29].
| Impact on Patient Outcomes

The choice of surgical technique, influenced by the disparities, directly impacts patient outcomes.Studies from across the region, such as those by Nguyen et al. and Pek et al., demonstrate that while advanced techniques like the DIEP flap offer better esthetic outcomes and lower complication rates, they are often inaccessible to many patients due to cost and availability [28,32].Conversely, techniques like the TRAM and LD flaps, while more widely available, carry higher risks of complications such as necrosis and infection, as observed in studies by Lokejareonlarb and Chamalerk [33] and Sriussadaporn and Angspatt [31].These complications can negatively impact patient satisfaction and longterm outcomes, underscoring the need for greater equity in access to advanced reconstruction options.
| Intersection of Cultural, Economic, and Medical Factors

The intersection of cultural, economic, and medical factors creates a multifaceted landscape in which decisions about breast reconstruction are made.Cultural norms heavily  influence how patients perceive reconstruction, with some cultures viewing it as unnecessary or even undesirable, leading to lower uptake rates.Economic limitations further compound these cultural barriers, particularly, in regions where healthcare costs are prohibitive and access to advanced surgical techniques is limited.

Medical factors, such as the stage of cancer at diagnosis and the availability of skilled surgeons, also play a critical role.In advanced cancer stages, as shown in Lim, Low, and Hoe, the need for aggressive adjuvant therapy often takes precedence over immediate reconstruction, leading to delays or the selection of less complex reconstruction methods [7].This medical necessity intersects with economic and cultural factors, making reconstruction an even less viable option for many women in the region.
| Systemic Healthcare Priorities and Their Impact on Breast Reconstruction Access

In addition to cultural and economic barriers, the low rate of breast reconstruction in Southeast Asia may reflect broader systemic deficiencies in healthcare delivery, particularly, in resourcelimited settings where life-saving interventions are prioritized [34][35][36][37].Procedures which are considered critical to immediate survival, are often given precedence over nonlife-saving surgeries like breast reconstruction.In impoverished healthcare systems, limited resources are allocated toward treatments that directly reduce mortality, leaving elective, or quality-of-life enhancing procedures, such as breast reconstruction, under-prioritized [38].This pattern suggests that the low rates of breast reconstruction may not be unique to this procedure, but part of a larger issue of inequitable healthcare distribution.Addressing these disparities requires not only improving access to breast reconstruction but also strengthening overall healthcare infrastructure to ensure comprehensive care that includes both life-saving and quality-oflife procedures [39][40][41][42][43][44][45][46][47].
| Implications for Practice and Policy

The findings from this systematic review underscore the pressing need for targeted interventions and policy changes to reduce disparities in breast reconstruction access and outcomes across Southeast Asia.Addressing the cultural, economic, and medical factors that contribute to these disparities is essential for improving the overall quality of breast cancer care in the region.By focusing on strategies that enhance access to information, expand reconstructive options, and support policy reform, healthcare providers and policymakers can make significant strides toward ensuring equitable care for all women undergoing breast cancer treatment.
| Targeted Interventions to Reduce Disparities

One of the most critical interventions needed is improving access to information about breast reconstruction.The review reveals that a significant barrier to reconstruction is the lack of awareness and understanding among patients, particularly, in culturally diverse and economically disadvantaged populations.

Studies like those by Shameem, Yip, and Fong and Soon et al. highlight how misinformation and cultural misconceptions about reconstruction contribute to lower uptake rates [8,19].To address this, healthcare providers must implement culturally sensitive educational programs that inform women about their reconstructive options, the benefits of reconstruction, and the potential risks [48].These programs should be designed to reach diverse populations, using multiple languages and culturally appropriate messaging to ensure that all women, regardless of their background, have access to the information they need to make informed decisions.

Expanding access to reconstructive options is another crucial area for intervention.The review indicates that advanced techniques like the DIEP flap, which offer superior esthetic outcomes and lower complication rates, are often inaccessible due to cost and limited availability [49].To bridge this gap, it is essential to invest in training more surgeons in these advanced techniques and establishing specialized centers that can offer a broader range of reconstructive options at affordable prices.Partnerships with international organizations and governments could also provide funding and resources to enhance the capabilities of local healthcare systems, ensuring that more women have access to high-quality reconstruction services [50].
| Limitations

This systematic review has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the findings.First, the inclusion criteria limited the search to studies published in English, which may have excluded relevant research published in other languages, particularly, in Southeast Asian countries where local languages are prevalent in academic publishing [51].This language bias could result in an incomplete picture of breast reconstruction practices and disparities in the region, potentially overlooking studies that provide valuable insights from non-English-speaking populations.

Second, the review relied on published studies, which may have introduced publication bias.Studies with significant or positive findings are more likely to be published, while those with negative or inconclusive results might be underrepresented.This could skew the understanding of the true extent of disparities and outcomes in breast reconstruction across Southeast Asia.

Third, the heterogeneity of the included studies in terms of study design, population, and outcome measures posed a challenge in synthesizing the data.Differences in healthcare systems, cultural practices, and economic conditions across the region further complicated comparisons between studies, potentially limiting the generalizability of the findings.

Finally, the majority of the studies included in the review were conducted in more developed parts of Southeast Asia, such as Singapore and Malaysia, which may not fully represent the experiences of women in less developed or rural areas where access to healthcare and breast reconstruction services might be even more limited.This geographic concentration could lead to an overestimation of access and outcomes in the region as a whole.Despite these limitations, the review provides a valuable synthesis of the available evidence and highlights critical areas for future research and policy development to address disparities in breast reconstruction in Southeast Asia.
| Conclusion

Addressing disparities in breast reconstruction across Southeast Asia is crucial to improving the quality of care and outcomes for women with breast cancer.This systematic review highlights significant gaps in access to reconstruction, shaped by cultural, economic, and medical factors, which collectively influence patient decisions and outcomes.These disparities result in unequal opportunities for women to benefit from reconstructive surgery, with those in disadvantaged or rural communities, or from certain cultural backgrounds, often facing greater barriers to accessing these life-enhancing procedures.

The findings underscore the need for culturally sensitive care that respects and responds to the diverse beliefs and preferences of women throughout the region [52].Healthcare providers must be attuned to the cultural factors that influence patient decisions, offering tailored information and support to ensure that every woman has the opportunity to make informed choices about her treatment.Culturally sensitive education and communication can help dispel myths, address fears, and empower women to consider reconstruction as a viable option in their recovery.

Equitable access to breast reconstruction is not just a matter of improving individual outcomes; it is a public health imperative [53].Policymakers and healthcare leaders must prioritize the integration of breast reconstruction into standard cancer care, ensuring that it is accessible to all women, regardless of their financial situation or geographic location.By reducing economic barriers, expanding the availability of advanced surgical techniques, and fostering multidisciplinary care teams that advocate for reconstruction as part of comprehensive cancer treatment, the region can make significant strides toward closing the gap in breast cancer care.

In conclusion, the pursuit of equitable, culturally sensitive breast reconstruction services in Southeast Asia is essential for enhancing the overall well-being of women with breast cancer.By addressing the disparities identified in this review, healthcare systems can ensure that all women could access the care they need to recover both physically and emotionally from breast cancer, ultimately improving survival rates and quality of life across the region.
